'''Hugh Hamilton''' {{post-nominals|FRS}} (26 March 1729 – 1 December 1805) was a mathematician, [[natural philosophy|natural philosopher]] (scientist) and professor at [[Trinity College Dublin]], and later a [[Church of Ireland]] bishop, [[Bishop of Clonfert and Kilmacduagh]] and then [[Bishop of Ossory]].

==Life==
He was born at Knock, near [[Balrothery]] in [[County Dublin]] (now [[Fingal]]), on 26 March 1729, the eldest son of Alexander (died 1768)<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.leighrayment.com/commons/irelandcommons.htm |title=Irish House of Commons 1692–1800 |first=Leigh |last=Rayment |work=Leigh Rayment's Peerage Page |access-date=23 December 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090601105535/http://www.leighrayment.com/commons/irelandcommons.htm |archive-date=1 June 2009 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Burke's Irish Family Records |edition=103 |page=546}}</ref> and Isabella Hamilton.<ref name=odnb/> His father was a solicitor and politician who represented the [[Killyleagh (Parliament of Ireland constituency)|Killyleagh constituency]] in the [[Irish House of Commons]] from 1739 to 1759.<ref name=house/> Alexander's great-grandfather Hugh Hamilton migrated from Scotland to [[County Down]] in the early 17th century. The Scottish architect [[James Hamilton of Finnart]] was an ancestor.<ref name=odnb/> Isabella Hamilton was born Isabella Maxwell, the daughter of Robert Maxwell of Finnebrogue, [[Downpatrick]].<ref name=house>{{cite book |title=A History of the House of Hamilton |last=Hamilton |first=George |year=1933 |publisher=J. Skinner & Co |location=Edinburgh |page=959}}</ref> Hugh's siblings included [[George Hamilton (Irish politician)|George Hamilton]],  Baron of the [[Court of Exchequer (Ireland)]] and Charles, father of the wealthy  Canadian lumber merchant and politician  [[George Hamilton (lumber baron)|George Hamilton]].

Hamilton entered [[Trinity College Dublin]] on 17 November 1742 at the age of 13 with Thomas McDonnell as his tutor. He graduated [[Bachelor of Arts]] (BA) in 1747 and [[Master of Arts (Oxbridge and Dublin)|Trinity Master of Arts]] (MA Dubl) in 1750.<ref name=odnb/> He took the competitive examination for a vacant fellowship of the college in 1750, but the position was secured instead by his friend [[Richard Murray (mathematician)|Richard Murray]], who was a few years older. Two fellowships became vacant the following year and Hamilton was elected to one of them at the age of 22.<ref name=life1809>{{cite book |last=Hamilton |first=Alexander |chapter=Life of the late Lord Bishop of Ossory |editor-last=Hamilton |editor-first=Alexander |title=The Works of the Right Rev. Hugh Hamilton, D.D., Late Bishop of Ossory |year=1809 |volume=I |page=viii–xv |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=MW5bAAAAQAAJ |access-date=3 October 2016}}</ref> He was appointed [[Erasmus Smith's Professor of Natural and Experimental Philosophy at Trinity College Dublin]] in 1759<ref>[https://www.maths.tcd.ie/about/400Hist/7.php Erasmus Smith's professors of Mathematics] Mathematics at TCD 1592–1992</ref> and that same year graduated [[Bachelor of Divinity]] (BD).<ref name=odnb/> He was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] on 19 February 1761<ref>{{cite web |url= http://royalsociety.org/uploadedFiles/Royal_Society_Content/about-us/fellowship/Fellows1660-2007.pdf |title=List of Fellows of the Royal Society 1660 - 2007 |date=July 2007 |publisher=The Royal Society |access-date=3 October 2016}}</ref> and graduated [[Doctor of Divinity]] (DD) in 1762.<ref name=odnb>{{cite encyclopedia |last=Blacker |first=B. H. |others=Revised by Philip Carter |encyclopedia=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography |title=Hamilton, Hugh (1729–1805) |url=http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/12076 |access-date=10 December 2011 |year=2004 |publisher=Oxford University Press |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/12076|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Trinity College presented him to the [[Rector (ecclesiastical)|rector]]y of [[Kilmacrenan]] in the diocese of [[Raphoe]], [[County Donegal]], in 1764. This was a small [[benefice|living]] in the gift of the college, for which he resigned his fellowship. He retained the Erasmus Smith's chair, however,<ref name=life1809/> being succeeded in that by Thomas Wilson in 1769.<ref name=400Hist_7>{{cite web |url= https://www.maths.tcd.ie/about/400Hist/7.php |title=400 years of mathematics: The eighteenth century |first=T.D. |last=Spearman |date=1992 |publisher=Trinity College Dublin |access-date=17 September 2016}}</ref> He resigned from Kilmacrenan in 1767 and become [[vicar]] of [[St. Ann's Church, Dawson Street|St. Anne's]] in Dublin.

He then became [[Dean of Armagh]], the chief resident cleric of [[St Patrick's Cathedral, Armagh (Church of Ireland)|St Patrick's Cathedral]] in [[Armagh]], from April 1768 to 1796.<ref name=odnb/> Finding the existing dean's house inconvenient and poorly situated, he had a new one built in a better location<ref name=life1809/> just off Portadown Road, now known as Dean's Hill. The house, of three stories and a semi-basement,<ref name=Armstrong/> was built in 1772–74.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bence-Jones |first=Mark |date=1978 |title=Burke's Guide to Country Houses |volume=1. Ireland |location=London |publisher=Burke's Peerage |page=[https://archive.org/details/burkesguidetocou00benc/page/100 100] |isbn=0850110262 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/burkesguidetocou00benc/page/100 }}</ref> The house was later sold by the church and the present owners provide bed and breakfast accommodation in it.<ref name=Armstrong>{{cite web |url= http://landedfamilies.blogspot.co.nz/2015/09/183-armstrong-and-wright-armstrong-of.html |title=Armstrong and Wright-Armstrong of Armagh and Killylea |first=Nick |last=Kingsley |date=20 September 2015 |work=Landed Families of Britain and Ireland |access-date=7 October 2016}}</ref> While dean he also acted as treasurer for the infirmary or county hospital, he established Sunday schools in the districts of the parish, and he founded a charitable loan for poor tradesmen. He was also instrumental in planning a piped water supply for the town, which was later put into effect.<ref name=life1809/> Hamilton was one of the 38 original members of the [[Royal Irish Academy]] when it was founded in 1785.<ref>{{cite book |last=Carlisle |first=Nicholas |date=1813 |title=An Index to The Transactions of the Royal Irish Academy |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=uWFFAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA96 |pages=96–97}}</ref> [[Gilbert Stuart]] painted his portrait in about 1790.<ref>[http://siris-artinventories.si.edu/ipac20/ipac.jsp?uri=full=3100001~!400223!0#focus "Hugh Hamilton, Dean of Armagh, (painting)"]. ''Art Inventories Catalog''. Smithsonian American Art Museum.</ref>

He was promoted to [[Bishop of Clonfert and Kilmacduagh]] on 20 January 1796, without seeking it.<ref name=history/> On 24 January 1799 he was [[translation (ecclesiastical)|translated]] to Ossory,<ref>''Handbook of British Chronology'' By Fryde, E. B; Greenway, D.E; Porter, S; Roy, I: Cambridge, [[Cambridge University Press|CUP]], 1996 {{ISBN|0-521-56350-X}}, 9780521563505</ref> where he was bishop until 1805.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thesilverbowl.com/documents/1801Aug17_OLIVER-HAMILTON.html#_ftn2|title=The Silver Bowl: 1801 August 17|website=Thesilverbowl.com|access-date=8 June 2016}}</ref> He died of a fever  at [[Kilkenny]] on 1 December 1805.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.libraryireland.com/biography/HughHamiltonBishopofOssory.php|title=Hugh Hamilton, Bishop of Ossory |website=Libraryireland.com |access-date=8 June 2016}}</ref> He was buried in the graveyard of [[St Canice's Cathedral]] at Kilkenny, and there is a memorial to him inside the cathedral.

==Works==
Hamilton wrote a mathematical treatise on conic sections called ''De Sectionibus Conicis: Tractatus Geometricus'', published in 1758.<ref name=odnb/> In this book he "was the first to deduce the properties of the conic section from the properties of the cone, by demonstrations which were general, unencumbered by lemmas, and proceeding in a more natural and perspicuous order", according to writer [[James Wills (poet)|James Wills]] in 1847.<ref name=history>{{cite book |title=A History of Ireland in the Lives of Irishmen |last=Wills |first=James |year=c. 1847 |publisher=Fullarton |location=London |url=https://archive.org/stream/historyofireland6_00will/historyofireland6_00will_djvu.txt |access-date=10 December 2011}}</ref> The work was acclaimed for its lucidity and [[Leonhard Euler]] described it as a perfect book.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |last=Florides |first=Petros S. |author-link=Petros Serghiou Florides |editor-last=McCartney |editor-first=Mark |editor2-last=Whitaker |editor2-first=Andrew |encyclopedia=Physicists of Ireland: Passion and Precision |title=John Synge 1897–1995 |year=2003 |publisher=Institute of Physics Pub. |page=210 }}</ref> It was "soon adopted in all the British universities"<ref name=history/> and was translated from Latin into English as ''A Geometrical Treatise of the Conic Sections'' in 1773.

He also wrote ''Philosophical Essays on Vapours'' (1767), ''Four Introductory Lectures on Natural Philosophy'' (1774), and ''An Essay on the Existence and Attributes of the Supreme Being'' (1784). His principal works were collected and republished, with a memoir, as ''The Works of the Right Rev. Hugh Hamilton'' by his eldest son, Alexander Hamilton, in two volumes in 1809.<ref name=odnb/>

==Family==
Hamilton married Isabella, daughter of Hans Widman Wood of Rosmead, [[County Westmeath]], in 1772. Isabella's mother Frances was the twin sister of [[Edward King, 1st Earl of Kingston]]. Hugh and Isabella had five sons and two daughters. They were Alexander, who was a [[barrister]]; Frances; Hans, who was rector of [[Knocktopher]] and associated with the [[Carrickshock incident]] of 1831; Isabella; Henry; [[George Hamilton (biblical scholar)|George]], who was a biblical scholar;<ref>{{cite DNB|wstitle=Hamilton, George (1783-1830)|volume=24}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=The Peerage of England, Scotland, and Ireland: The peerage of Ireland|url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_RtsWAAAAYAAJ|year=1790|publisher=W. Owen [and 2 others]|page=[https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_RtsWAAAAYAAJ/page/n233 136]}}</ref> and Hugh,<ref>{{cite DNB|wstitle=Hamilton, Hugh (1729-1805)|volume=24}}</ref> who married Elizabeth Staples, a daughter of [[John Staples]], a Member of Parliament. The younger Hugh was the great-grandfather of Clive Staples Lewis, better known as [[C. S. Lewis]].<ref>''The Collected Letters of C. S. Lewis''. Vol. I, pg. 996. Ed. Walter Hooper.</ref> Bishop Hugh Hamilton was a great-great-great-grandfather of the mathematicians [[John Lighton Synge]] and his brother [[Edward Hutchinson Synge]].<ref>''[https://www.tcd.ie/Secretary/FellowsScholars/discourses/discourses/2009_P%20Florides%20on%20J%20L%20Synge.pdf John Lighton Synge]'' by Petros S. Florides, School of Mathematics, Trinity College Dublin</ref> [[Dodgson Hamilton Madden]], the High Court judge and noted scholar, was the Bishop's great-grandson.
